questions.stem: A 78 year old woman is on the orthopaedic ward 7 days after a hip hemiarthroplasty. She received cefuroxime and takes omeprazole. She now has 7 episodes a day of green, foul-smelling watery stool with mucus, cramps and nausea. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Her abdomen is diffusely tender but not distended.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Foul-smelling green watery diarrhoea with mucus, cramps and diffuse tenderness after a cephalosporin, post-operatively and on a PPI, is C. difficile infection (pseudomembranous colitis).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: green, foul-smelling watery stool with mucus
steps.x: Antibiotics + PPI + foul watery diarrhoea = C. difficile.

elim: Left iliac fossa pain and fever, not profuse watery diarrhoea after antibiotics.
Sudden pain with bloody diarrhoea in vascular patients.
Prominent vomiting with ward outbreaks, short-lived, unrelated to antibiotics.
Small-volume leakage with a loaded rectum, not foul green watery stool with fever.

steps.x: A: Clostridioides difficile infection. Cephalosporins and PPIs are classic C. difficile risk factors.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man has toxin-positive C. difficile infection. He finished a course of amoxicillin 2 weeks ago. His regular medicines are amlodipine, metformin, omeprazole, paracetamol and ramipril. The ward pharmacist reviews his drug chart to reduce his risk of recurrence.
questions.q: Which of his regular medicines most increases his risk of C. difficile infection?
questions.e: Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole are implicated in C. difficile infection; stopping an unnecessary PPI reduces recurrence.

steps.x: The question asks: Which of his regular medicines most increases his risk of C. difficile infection?
PPIs are the non-antibiotic drug to stop.

elim: Not linked with C. difficile.
Causes loose stools but not C. difficile.
Not a risk factor.
Not a risk factor.

steps.x: C: Omeprazole. PPIs and antibiotics predispose to C. difficile.

questions.stem: A 4 year old boy at a nursery where several children have diarrhoea has 2 days of high fever, cramping abdominal pain and frequent small stools containing blood and mucus. He had a brief febrile seizure this morning. His temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 140 bpm, BP 94/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Stool microscopy shows many pus cells. Stool culture grows a non-motile, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Bloody mucoid diarrhoea with high fever, febrile seizure and nursery spread, with a non-motile non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod, is Shigella: a classic bacterial cause of bloody diarrhoea and fever.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely causative organism?

clues: nursery where several children have diarrhoea
steps.x: Nursery outbreak, dysentery, febrile seizure = Shigella.

elim: A curved, motile Gram-negative rod linked to poultry.
A Gram-positive anaerobe after antibiotics.
A protozoan in travellers, with a slower onset.
Watery, not bloody, diarrhoea in infants.

steps.x: E: Shigella sonnei. Shigella: bloody diarrhoea and fever.

questions.stem: A 9 year old girl has 3 days of crampy abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea that began 4 days after eating an undercooked burger at a barbecue. She has had no fever. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 100/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. Her abdomen is tender in both iliac fossae. Stool culture on sorbitol MacConkey agar grows non-sorbitol-fermenting colonies.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Bloody diarrhoea, often with little fever, after undercooked beef, with non-sorbitol-fermenting colonies is E. coli O157 (Shiga toxin-producing). It is important because of the risk of haemolytic uraemic syndrome.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely causative organism?
Undercooked beef + bloody diarrhoea + sorbitol-negative = E. coli O157.

elim: Usually from poultry, with fever.
Vomiting and watery diarrhoea, not bloody.
Usually febrile, from eggs and poultry, and ferments sorbitol.
Toxin-mediated vomiting within hours.

steps.x: B: Escherichia coli O157. E. coli is a bacterial cause of bloody diarrhoea.

questions.stem: Twelve hours after eating a homemade tiramisu made with raw eggs, a 34 year old woman develops fever, headache, cramping abdominal pain and diarrhoea, now with some blood. Four other guests are similarly unwell. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 110/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Her abdomen is diffusely tender.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Fever, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea (sometimes bloody) 12 to 72 hours after raw eggs, in a cluster, is non-typhoidal Salmonella colitis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely causative organism?
Raw eggs, 12 to 72 hours, fever and diarrhoea = Salmonella.

elim: Vomiting within hours of reheated rice.
Linked to undercooked poultry, with a longer incubation of 2 to 5 days.
Follows antibiotics, not a shared meal.
Travel-related and slower in onset.

steps.x: E: Salmonella enteritidis. Salmonella: bloody diarrhoea and fever, eggs and poultry.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man returned from 2 months working in rural Mexico. Over 4 weeks he has developed loose stools with blood and mucus, mild lower abdominal pain and tiredness, without a high fever. His temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 86 bpm, BP 124/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. Colonoscopy shows scattered ulcers with normal mucosa between them; biopsies show flask-shaped ulcers with trophozoites containing red cells.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Gradual-onset bloody diarrhoea after travel, with flask-shaped ulcers and erythrophagocytic trophozoites, is amoebic colitis (Entamoeba histolytica), a parasitic cause of infectious colitis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Travel + subacute bloody diarrhoea + trophozoites = amoebic colitis.

elim: Acute onset with fever after poultry, usually resolving within a week.
Granulomas on biopsy, without trophozoites.
Acute high fever with dysentery.
Continuous inflammation from the rectum, no organisms.

steps.x: A: Amoebic colitis. Parasitic colitis: bloody diarrhoea with a travel history.

questions.stem: A 21 year old student has 2 days of fever, colicky abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea. He cooked chicken on a disposable barbecue 3 days before. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. Stool microscopy shows curved, S-shaped Gram-negative rods with darting motility. He is drinking well.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Curved 'seagull' Gram-negative rods after undercooked poultry with fever and bloody diarrhoea is Campylobacter, the commonest bacterial cause in the UK. It is usually self-limiting.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely causative organism?
Poultry + curved rods = Campylobacter.

elim: Gram-positive; follows antibiotics.
Straight rods, linked to beef and usually afebrile.
A protozoan causing non-bloody greasy diarrhoea.
Painless rice-water stools, not bloody diarrhoea.

steps.x: A: Campylobacter jejuni. Campylobacter is usually self-limiting.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man develops 5 watery stools a day 4 days after starting piperacillin-tazobactam for pneumonia. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 126/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. His abdomen is mildly tender. Investigations: C. difficile glutamate dehydrogenase (antigen) positive; C. difficile toxin positive; WCC 11.2 ×10⁹/L (4–11).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate interpretation of these results?
questions.e: C. difficile antigen positivity alone shows colonisation (exposure). Toxin positivity is needed to show true infection, and here both are positive with symptoms.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate interpretation of these results?
Antigen = exposure; toxin = infection.

elim: Antigen alone would mean colonisation; toxin positivity shows true infection.
No reason to doubt it with typical symptoms.
No hypotension, ileus or megacolon.
WCC is not over 15 and there is no creatinine rise.

steps.x: A: Active C. difficile infection. Toxin positivity confirms active infection.

questions.stem: An 83 year old woman has toxin-positive C. difficile infection with 6 stools a day. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Her abdomen is tender but soft, with bowel sounds present. Investigations: WCC 12.4 ×10⁹/L (4–11); creatinine 156 µmol/L (45–90), baseline 88 µmol/L 1 month ago.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate assessment of severity?
questions.e: Severe C. difficile infection is WCC over 15 ×10⁹/L or an acute creatinine rise of more than 50% above baseline. Her creatinine has risen by about 77%, even though the WCC is under 15.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most accurate assessment of severity?
Either WCC over 15 or creatinine up by over 50% = severe.

elim: She is toxin positive with symptoms.
No hypotension, ileus, toxic megacolon or CT dilatation.
The creatinine rise makes it severe.
A creatinine rise of over 50% classes it as severe.

steps.x: E: Severe infection. Severity markers: WCC >15, creatinine rise >50%.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man with C. difficile infection becomes drowsy. His stools have slowed and his abdomen is distended and tympanic with absent bowel sounds. His temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 126 bpm, BP 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. Lactate is 4.6 mmol/L. CT abdomen shows the transverse colon dilated to 8 cm with mucosal thickening.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Life-threatening C. difficile infection with toxic megacolon
questions.e: Shock, ileus and colonic dilatation on CT in C. difficile infection is life-threatening disease with toxic megacolon. It needs oral vancomycin plus IV metronidazole and urgent surgical review.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Septic, ileus, dilated colon = life-threatening CDI.

elim: Vomiting with dilated small bowel loops, not a dilated colon in active colitis.
Left iliac fossa collection on CT.
Colonic dilatation without colitis or sepsis.
A coffee-bean loop with a twist, not colitis.

steps.x: C: Life-threatening C. difficile infection with toxic megacolon. Life-threatening CDI: oral vancomycin and IV metronidazole.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman with severe C. difficile infection was prescribed loperamide by the night team for frequent stools, and continues codeine phosphate for knee pain. Over 24 hours her stools have stopped and her abdomen has become distended and very tender. Her colon measures 7 cm on X-ray.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her deterioration?
o: Loperamide and codeine precipitating toxic megacolon
questions.e: Opioids and antimotility agents (loperamide, codeine) slow the colon and predispose to toxic megacolon in C. difficile colitis. They should be stopped.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her deterioration?
Diarrhoea stops + belly swells after antimotility drugs = toxic megacolon.

elim: Does not cause acute colonic dilatation with tenderness in active colitis.
Stopping diarrhoea with distension is a warning sign, not recovery.
She has a dilated colon.
No history of UC.

steps.x: B: Loperamide and codeine precipitating toxic megacolon. Halt opioids and antimotility drugs in CDI.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has had profuse watery diarrhoea for 10 days after clindamycin for a dental abscess. He is admitted and a flexible sigmoidoscopy is performed before stool results are available. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 120/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding at sigmoidoscopy?
o: Contact bleeding with continuous granular mucosa from the rectum
Deep serpiginous ulcers with skip lesions
Raised yellow plaques on inflamed mucosa
questions.e: Clindamycin is a classic cause of C. difficile infection; toxins cause pseudomembranes, seen as raised yellow plaques on the mucosa.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding at sigmoidoscopy?
C. difficile on endoscopy = yellow pseudomembranes.

elim: Ulcerative colitis.
Crohn's disease.
Incidental finding.
Unlikely with toxin-mediated colitis this severe.

steps.x: E: Raised yellow plaques on inflamed mucosa. Pseudomembranes: raised yellow plaques.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman with ulcerative colitis, in remission on mesalazine, took ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection 10 days ago. She now has 8 watery stools a day with cramps. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 114/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Stool testing shows C. difficile toxin. Sigmoidoscopy shows inflamed mucosa with yellow plaques.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.e: Ulcerative colitis and recent antibiotics (ciprofloxacin) are risk factors for C. difficile infection. Patients with IBD and a flare should always have stool tested for C. difficile.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
UC 'flare' after antibiotics: think C. difficile.

elim: Her diagnosis is established UC and toxin is positive.
Does not cause fever, toxin positivity or plaques.
She has taken it for years without problems.
The toxin and pseudomembranes point to C. difficile.

steps.x: A: Clostridioides difficile infection. UC is a risk factor for C. difficile.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man who had a kidney transplant 4 months ago takes tacrolimus and mycophenolate. He has 10 days of bloody diarrhoea, fever and abdominal pain. Stool cultures and C. difficile toxin are negative. Colonoscopy shows patchy ulceration, and biopsies show large cells with 'owl's eye' intranuclear inclusions.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Infectious colitis can be bacterial, viral or parasitic. In an immunosuppressed transplant patient, bloody diarrhoea with owl's eye inclusions is cytomegalovirus colitis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Immunosuppression + owl's eye inclusions = CMV colitis.

elim: Trophozoites with flask-shaped ulcers after travel.
Sudden pain with segmental change in vascular patients; no inclusions.
Possible, but owl's eye inclusions show viral infection.
Toxin is negative and no plaques are seen.

steps.x: B: Cytomegalovirus colitis. Viruses are a cause of infectious colitis.

questions.stem: A 80 year old man on the medical ward develops frequent watery diarrhoea after a course of co-amoxiclav. A stool sample has been sent for C. difficile testing and he has been moved to a side room. His temperature is 37.7°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. He has a dry tongue.
questions.q: Which are the most appropriate initial blood tests?
o: Full blood count, CRP and U&Es
questions.e: First-line bloods are FBC (raised WCC, a severity marker), CRP and U&Es (dehydration and a creatinine rise that defines severity).

steps.x: The question asks: Which are the most appropriate initial blood tests?
FBC, CRP, U&Es: infection, severity, kidneys.

elim: For pancreatitis.
Not helpful here.
Not the priority.
Not relevant to acute infective diarrhoea.

steps.x: D: Full blood count, CRP and U&Es. Bloods: FBC, CRP, U&Es.

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman in a care home has 4 days of watery diarrhoea with cramps after a course of cefalexin. She takes lansoprazole. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 94 bpm, BP 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Her abdomen is mildly tender. The GP wants to confirm the cause.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: C. difficile toxin and culture on a stool sample
questions.e: The gold standard is stool culture and toxin testing. Toxin positivity confirms active infection rather than colonisation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
Suspected C. difficile = stool for toxin.

elim: Shows dilatation but cannot confirm infection.
C. difficile does not cause bacteraemia.
Not needed and risks perforation.
Non-specific marker of inflammation.

steps.x: C: C. difficile toxin and culture on a stool sample. Stool culture and toxin testing.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman returned 3 weeks ago from a year teaching in rural Bangladesh. She has had 2 weeks of loose stools with blood and mucus, mild abdominal pain and no fever. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. She has had no antibiotics.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Microscopy, culture and PCR of stool
questions.e: Bloody diarrhoea after travel needs stool microscopy (for ova, cysts and parasites such as Entamoeba histolytica), culture and PCR.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
Travel-related dysentery = stool microscopy, culture and PCR.

elim: Does not identify the organism.
No antibiotic exposure; travel points to other organisms.
Stool testing comes first.
For pancreatitis.

steps.x: D: Microscopy, culture and PCR of stool. Stool culture and PCR.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man has toxin-positive C. difficile infection. His creatinine is stable at baseline. He is passing 6 loose stools a day and has mild tenderness. His team tracks one blood marker each day to decide whether he meets criteria for severe disease. The trend is shown.

visual.title: Daily blood marker
visual.caption: Rising above 15 ×10⁹/L: now severe C. difficile infection.

questions.q: Which investigation is being used to judge his severity?
questions.e: WCC is the marker of severity in C. difficile infection: over 15 ×10⁹/L (or a creatinine rise of over 50%) means severe disease. His has crossed 15 on day 3.

steps.x: The question asks: Which investigation is being used to judge his severity?
WCC over 15 = severe.

elim: Falls with illness but is not a severity criterion.
Rises with inflammation but is not the defining marker.
Not a severity marker in C. difficile.
A marker of shock in life-threatening disease, not the routine severity marker.

steps.x: C: Full blood count (white cell count). WCC marks severity.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man who works as a chef has 2 days of fever and bloody diarrhoea after eating at a street food stall. He has had no antibiotics and has not travelled. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. His employer needs to know whether he can return to food handling.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Bacterial colitis (Campylobacter, Shigella, Salmonella, E. coli) is identified by stool culture and PCR, which also guides exclusion advice for food handlers.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
Community bloody diarrhoea = stool culture and PCR.

elim: Not routinely needed.
May be positive in Salmonella but miss most causes.
No antibiotic or hospital exposure.
Not first-line in acute infective diarrhoea.

steps.x: E: Stool culture and PCR. Stool culture and PCR identify bacterial causes.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has toxin-positive C. difficile infection while on day 5 of co-amoxiclav for a chest infection that has now clinically resolved. Her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 92 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Her WCC is 13 ×10⁹/L. Oral vancomycin has been prescribed.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Start a probiotic and continue co-amoxiclav
questions.e: Stop the causative antibiotic whenever possible. Her chest infection has resolved, so co-amoxiclav is stopped alongside oral vancomycin.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
Stop the culprit antibiotic.

elim: Antimotility drugs risk toxic megacolon.
Another broad-spectrum antibiotic that perpetuates C. difficile.
Ongoing antibiotics worsen C. difficile.
The causative antibiotic should be stopped.

steps.x: D: Discontinue co-amoxiclav. Stop the causative antibiotic if possible.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man has a first episode of toxin-positive C. difficile infection with 6 stools a day and a WCC of 16 ×10⁹/L. His creatinine is at baseline. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. He has no ileus or hypotension. The foundation doctor suggests intravenous vancomycin.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Moderate-to-severe C. difficile infection is treated first-line with oral vancomycin for 10 days. It must be oral because IV vancomycin does not reach the colon.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
C. difficile: vancomycin by mouth, 10 days.

elim: Reserved, with oral vancomycin, for life-threatening disease.
IV vancomycin is not excreted into the colon lumen.
Would worsen C. difficile.
Risks toxic megacolon.

steps.x: E: Oral vancomycin for 10 days. First-line: oral vancomycin for 10 days.

questions.stem: An 82 year old woman with C. difficile infection is in a side room on day 6 of oral vancomycin. Her last loose stool was 20 hours ago and she now has formed stools. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 80 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. The bed manager wants to move her back to the open bay today.
questions.q: When is it most appropriate to end her isolation?
o: After a negative repeat toxin test
questions.e: Patients stay isolated until they have had no diarrhoea for at least 48 hours.

steps.x: The question asks: When is it most appropriate to end her isolation?

clues: Her last loose stool was 20 hours ago
back to the open bay today
steps.x: Isolation ends 48 hours after the last diarrhoea.

elim: Toxin can stay positive after recovery; clearance tests are not used.
Not yet 48 hours symptom-free.
Isolation is guided by symptoms, not the course.
Unnecessarily long.

steps.x: A: After 48 hours without diarrhoea. Isolate until 48 hours without diarrhoea.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with toxin-positive C. difficile infection has completed 7 days of oral vancomycin and is still passing 8 watery stools a day. The causative antibiotic was stopped. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 120/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. His abdomen is soft, with no distension or ileus.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: If C. difficile does not respond to oral vancomycin, or recurs within 12 weeks of resolution, oral fidaxomicin is second-line.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
Vancomycin failure = fidaxomicin.

elim: Considered after multiple recurrences, not after first-line failure.
Does not reach the colon.
Risks toxic megacolon.
No longer recommended for treatment in the UK.

steps.x: C: Oral fidaxomicin. Second-line: oral fidaxomicin.

questions.stem: A 77 year old woman with C. difficile infection did not respond to oral vancomycin and has now had 10 days of oral fidaxomicin, but still has 7 watery stools a day. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. There is no ileus, hypotension or colonic dilatation on imaging.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next treatment?
o: Oral vancomycin with or without IV metronidazole
questions.e: If there is still no response after fidaxomicin, oral vancomycin with or without IV metronidazole is tried again, with specialist input.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next treatment?

clues: did not respond to oral vancomycin
steps.x: Failed vancomycin then fidaxomicin = back to oral vancomycin ± IV metronidazole.

elim: Would worsen the infection.
Risks toxic megacolon.
She still has active infection.
For life-threatening disease failing medical therapy.

steps.x: C: Oral vancomycin with or without IV metronidazole. Third step: oral vancomycin ± IV metronidazole.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man is admitted with diarrhoea after recent antibiotics. Stool tests confirm C. difficile toxin. He is in a four-bed bay. A healthcare assistant has been cleaning her hands with alcohol gel between patients and asks what else is needed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate infection control measure?
o: Alcohol gel only, used more often
Continue in the bay with curtains drawn
Isolation in a side room with gloves, aprons and soap and water
Screen all patients in the bay with rectal swabs
questions.e: C. difficile needs side room isolation, single-use gloves and aprons, and hand washing with soap and water, because alcohol gel does not kill the spores.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate infection control measure?
Spores beat alcohol: isolate, gloves, aprons, soap and water.

elim: Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores.
Spores spread through the environment.
C. difficile is not airborne.
Not standard practice.

steps.x: D: Isolation in a side room with gloves, aprons and soap and water. Side room, PPE, soap and water.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman has 3 days of diarrhoea with some blood, cramps and mild fever after a barbecue. Stool culture grows Campylobacter jejuni. She is drinking but feels lightheaded on standing. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 116/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. She is not pregnant and is not immunosuppressed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral loperamide and stay off work 1 day
questions.e: Campylobacter is usually self-limiting. Oral rehydration solution is first-line; antibiotics are only given if severe.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?
Mild Campylobacter: rehydrate orally, no antibiotics.

elim: Reserved for patients who cannot keep up with oral fluids.
Antibiotics are only for severe disease; resistance is common.
Only if severe or in high-risk groups.
Antimotility agents are avoided in bloody diarrhoea.

steps.x: E: Oral rehydration solution. Rehydration: ORS first-line.

questions.stem: An 86 year old woman has had profuse watery diarrhoea for 3 days from C. difficile infection and has started oral vancomycin. She is vomiting and cannot keep oral fluids down. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Her mucous membranes are dry and her creatinine has risen.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate fluid management?
questions.e: Oral rehydration is first-line, but when patients cannot tolerate it or are hypotensive, IV fluids (0.9% saline) are given.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate fluid management?
Cannot drink + hypotensive = IV 0.9% saline.

elim: She cannot keep oral fluids down.
Not for simple dehydration.
Not a resuscitation fluid; worsens hyponatraemia.
Too slow for a hypotensive patient.

steps.x: B: Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride. IV 0.9% saline if oral rehydration fails.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has 8 days of bloody diarrhoea up to 10 times a day with high fevers. Stool culture grows Campylobacter jejuni. His temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 104/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. He is receiving IV fluids. His symptoms are not improving.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
questions.e: Campylobacter is usually self-limiting, but severe or prolonged infection is treated with a macrolide such as clarithromycin.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
Severe Campylobacter = clarithromycin.

elim: Not reliable for Campylobacter and promotes C. difficile.
For anaerobes and amoebae, not Campylobacter.
A urinary antibiotic.
For C. difficile.

steps.x: A: Clarithromycin. Severe Campylobacter: clarithromycin.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman on the stroke ward has 2 loose stools a day after starting senna and lactulose for constipation. She has had no antibiotics for 3 months. She is afebrile with a soft, non-tender abdomen. Stool test: C. difficile antigen positive, toxin negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Review the laxatives and monitor without C. difficile treatment
questions.e: Antigen positivity with a negative toxin means colonisation (exposure), not infection. Her loose stools are explained by laxatives, so no C. difficile treatment is needed.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?
Antigen only = colonisation: do not treat.

elim: Second-line treatment for infection, not colonisation.
Not indicated; she does not have active infection.
Treats active infection, which she does not have.
Not needed; the laxatives explain the stools.

questions.stem: A microbiology registrar explains why C. difficile survives on hospital surfaces for months and grows in the colon but not in routine aerobic blood culture bottles. On Gram staining of a culture grown in an anaerobic cabinet it appears as large purple rods, some containing spores.
questions.q: Which best describes this organism?
questions.e: C. difficile is an anaerobic, Gram-positive, spore-forming bacillus. The spores survive on surfaces and resist alcohol.

steps.x: C: Anaerobic spore-forming Gram-positive rod. C. difficile is an anaerobic Gram-positive bacterium.

questions.stem: An 80 year old woman develops C. difficile infection 6 days after starting IV cefuroxime for pneumonia. She had been in hospital a week, and the organism is common on the ward environment. A student asks why the antibiotic led to the infection.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Direct toxicity of cefuroxime to colonocytes
Disruption of normal colonic flora allowing spores to germinate
Reduced gastric acid killing of bacteria
questions.e: Broad-spectrum antibiotics disrupt the normal colonic flora, removing competition and allowing ingested C. difficile spores to germinate and proliferate.

questions.stem: After a cluster of C. difficile cases, a hospital restricts the use of cephalosporins, clindamycin and ciprofloxacin, and pharmacists review every antibiotic prescription at 48 hours. o: Increased use of proton pump inhibitors
Preserved colonic flora through antibiotic stewardship
questions.e: Antibiotic stewardship (avoiding broad-spectrum high-risk antibiotics and reviewing need) preserves the normal colonic flora, which is central to preventing C. difficile infection.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with severe C. difficile colitis develops toxic megacolon. The surgical registrar explains to a student why inflammation of the colon can lead to massive dilatation and why surgery may be needed urgently if it does not settle.
questions.q: Which best explains the progression and its main danger?
o: Mechanical obstruction by pseudomembranes causing closed-loop obstruction
Mucosal-only inflammation causing increased motility and bleeding
Neurological damage to the spinal cord
Transmural inflammation impairing motility and wall integrity, risking perforation
questions.e: Severe transmural inflammation impairs colonic motility and structural integrity, causing dilatation (toxic megacolon) and risking perforation and sepsis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best explains the progression and its main danger?
Full-thickness inflammation = paralysed, thin colon = perforation.

steps.x: D: Transmural inflammation impairing motility and wall integrity, risking perforation. Toxic megacolon risks perforation and sepsis.

questions.stem: Two patients on the same ward carry C. difficile. One has profuse diarrhoea and pseudomembranes; the other has formed stools. Laboratory testing shows that only the first patient's strain produces the organism's key virulence factors, and only his stool is positive for them.
questions.q: Which explains why only the first patient has colitis?

His strain secretes an IgA protease
questions.e: C. difficile damages colonic mucosal cells through toxins A and B. Non-toxigenic strains colonise without disease, which is why toxin positivity is needed to diagnose true infection.
